Algerian Border Tensions Disrupt Economy, Energy Sector Faces Strain

Algiers – Ongoing border tensions between Algeria and Morocco have escalated into a full-blown crisis, leading to heightened military activity and new cross-border restrictions. The situation, which began with a series of diplomatic disputes in late May, intensified last week after reported skirmishes near the Tindouf region, prompting the Algerian government to impose emergency controls on the movement of goods and people across its western frontier.

The disruption is reverberating throughout Algeria’s economy, with broad impacts on logistics, trade, and energy distribution. Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA, the national electricity and gas provider, is among the major companies reporting operational challenges. “We are experiencing significant delays in deliveries of critical equipment and spare parts, which are sourced through border crossings now closed or heavily restricted,” said a spokesperson for Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA. The company noted that ongoing maintenance projects at key generation facilities in Oran and Béchar have been postponed, raising concerns about grid reliability as summer demand peaks.

Analysts warn that the crisis could have lasting consequences. “Algeria relies on regional supply chains for everything from industrial components to basic foodstuffs,” said Mourad Bensaid, an economic consultant based in Algiers. “The sudden clampdown at the Moroccan border has disrupted not only direct imports, but also transit flows from European suppliers, putting pressure on inventories across multiple sectors.”

The Algerian Chamber of Commerce reported a 28% fall in cross-border freight volumes since the restrictions began, with local manufacturing and agricultural exporters expressing alarm over halted shipments and rising input costs. Labor unions representing transport and port workers in Ghazaouet and Maghnia have called for urgent government intervention, warning that prolonged disruption could lead to layoffs and wage delays.

As the crisis enters its third week, the government has pledged to bolster domestic supply chains and prioritize essential services. “National solidarity is paramount in these challenging times,” said Minister of Economy Nabil Kherbache during a televised address. “We are mobilizing resources to ensure the continuity of electricity, gas, and vital goods for all Algerians.”
